bbc_card_1.headline: Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital after smoke seen rising near Riyadh airport
bbc_card_1.description: The King Khalid International Airport incident caused hours of flight disruptions and comes amid an escalating conflict with Houthi rebels in Yemen.
bbc_card_1.article_content:
Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh and energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.

A column of black smoke was seen rising from what appeared to be fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport where flights were disrupted temporarily.

City residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors, the first such alert since a recent escalation in the conflict with the Houthis.

There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities.

In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast.

He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa.

Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.

The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.

According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.

The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.

On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796.

A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations.

An AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco.

The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.

Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.

The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.

Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

bbc_card_2.headline: Journalists denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
bbc_card_2.description: CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters' White House press badges were confiscated, the outlets reported.
bbc_card_2.article_content:
Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets.

An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported.

Both CNN and Politico also said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized.

Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

"The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.

CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.

Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass.

All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.

An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".

MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".

Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights.

And CNN said, "We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."

In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."

The White House Correspondents Association (WHCA) - the independent, non-profit group that represents journalists who cover the US presidency - called on the administration "to immediately restore" access to the journalists and accused it of violating the First Amendment.

"The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," said WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich, who works for Fox News.

Heinrich said that the Americans, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected in their coverage "regardless of whether government officials view it favorably".

"That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called Trump's White House ban illegal and unconstitutional.

A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.

It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

bbc_card_3.headline: Ed Sheeran set to play first concert since Macklemore controversy
bbc_card_3.description: The show in Philadelphia comes after rapper Macklemore was dropped  Ed Sheeran's tour over pro-Palestinian comments.
bbc_card_3.article_content:
British singer Ed Sheeran is performing his first show since facing backlash over a controversial decision to drop rapper Macklemore from his tour.

The decision - which Sheeran said was made by his promoter, not by himself - stemmed from pro-Palestinian comments Macklemore made on stage earlier this month.

The debacle has caused Sheeran's ticket sales to decline, supporting acts to drop out, and fans to express frustration.

But on Saturday morning outside the massive football stadium in Philadelphia, where the concert will be held, there is little to indicate an international rockstar will later be taking the stage.

Digital billboards surrounding Lincoln Financial Field, the venue, have no signage for the star and the streets are empty except for a smattering of news crews.

After Sheeran's opening acts all dropped out, the concert start time was pushed back to 20:00 local time (01:00 BST) - nearly three hours later than originally planned.

Meanwhile, pro-Palestinian groups are planning to protest outside the concert venue.

Here's what to know about the story.

While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel.

The following night, Macklemore referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects.

In response, the Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour, and the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda.

Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining her criticism of the rapper's comments.

Macklemore then posted on Instagram that the media attention "surrounding Pink and what I said" had caused billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft to call Sheeran.

"Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium," Macklemore wrote of Kraft, who also owns the New England Patriots American football team.

Concert promoter Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would cancel Sheeran's planned concerts if Macklemore remained on the bill.

Kraft, who is Jewish, confirmed he banned the US rapper from performing at Gillette, accusing Macklemore of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric.

"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.

Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's tour on 14 September.

The rapper said in a lengthy Instagram statement that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup.

Sheeran said the call was made by Messina Touring Group. The Bad Habits and Shape of You singer said he respected "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", adding that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way".

In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran was in but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.

"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.

The rapper, who in 2014 apologised for a costume he wore on stage which critics said was anti-Semitic, also addressed the accusations of antisemitism, writing that "one of the most effective ways to enforce silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism".

In his statement earlier this week, Sheeran said: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."

The singer-songwriter also said he did not want to let down his fans or crew by cancelling the tour.

Sheeran fans and ticket holders are torn about the situation. Some have said that without all the supporting acts, the show is no longer what they paid for.

Damien Given, who is from Northern Ireland and has tickets to Saturday's show, told the BBC that he felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans.

Given said that Sheeran can't suddenly say he's not political because he had previously voiced support for Ukraine after Russia invaded the country.

But another fan named Patti Ann told the BBC that Sheeran was in a "no-win situation".

"I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things."

The controversy has also snowballed into other areas of Sheeran's career. Ireland's Classic Hits Radio announced it was removing Sheeran's music from its playlists because of feedback from listeners who had expressed "disappointment and concern" over his US tour. Sheeran was raised in England but has said he identifies culturally as Irish.

Ticket resale prices for the singer's remaining US concert dates have decreased since the controversy began, with some going for below market value ahead of Saturday's concert, according to TicketData, a ticket sale tracking site.

Thousands of seats for the show are still available on Ticketmaster.

Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham, American singer-songwriter Finneas, and Irish folk band Beoga quit Sheeran's tour following Macklemore's departure.

In a post on Instagram, Rowe thanked Sheeran for the opportunity but said he "cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power" to silence people who criticise Israel's actions in Gaza. "Free Palestine," he added.

Lukas Graham similarly thanked Sheeran while expressing support for Palestinians and saying the band cannot "carry on with this tour as things stand".

Finneas, the brother of pop star Billie Eilish, said artists should "not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed".

Beoga, which had been serving as Sheeran's backing band, said they support Macklemore's message.

Sheeran's upcoming concert at Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday is the first show since Macklemore was dropped from the tour.

There are currently no opening or supporting acts publicly announced for Saturday's show.

Pro-Palestinian groups including Philly Palestine Coalition and Shut Down D&Z are organising a protest on Saturday near the stadium

"There is no neutrality against oppression, only complicity," they said in a post on Instagram.

Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour began in January 2026 with shows in New Zealand and Australia before he moved on to the Caribbean, Central America and South America.

On the US and Canadian leg of the tour, which began in Arizona in June, Sheeran has performed in a number of cities including Toronto, Denver, Seattle, Minneapolis and Los Angeles.

After the Philadelphia concert on Saturday, Sheeran has 10 remaining shows in the US through November, including Atlanta and Tampa. He then continues on to South America and wraps up in Mexico in December.

Additional reporting from Gabriela Pomeroy, Steven McIntosh, Brandon Drenon and Mark Savage.

card_1.headline: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
card_1.description: The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die.
card_1.article_content:
The summer (June to August) of 2026 was the warmest in Europe since records began, beating the record set in 2003, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service,

Not only that, Germany's DWD weather service says that there was an "unprecedented" number of hot days this year. "On average across Germany,there were about 22 hot days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees Celsius and about five very hot days with temperatures of at least 35 degrees Celsius," the DWD wrote in in a press release at the end of August.

The estimated number of heat-related deaths also reached unprecedented levels, with at least 16,300 people dying by the end of August, even if few of them died directly because of the heat, but rather as a consequence of underlying health conditions exacerbated by the heat.

The figures were compiled from a statistical correlation between the number of deaths recorded by Germany's Federal Statistical Office and the temperatures measured by the DWD during a specific period.

Heat-related deaths in Germany are more likely if the average weekly temperature reaches 20 degrees Celsius or more. This is the average of all hourly temperatures recorded in a week, including at nighttime.

This year, the average weekly temperatures in the country rose above the 20-degree mark several times. It was particularly hot at the end of June, when the average weekly temperature reached above 26 degrees between the 22nd and 28th of the month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Though it is not possible to determine a cause of death using statistics, researchers and medical professionals have a good understanding of how heat affects the human body, and there is widespread consensus that excess mortality during heat waves is possible.

"It was not just the high temperatures on the thermometer that were important, but also how long the heat lasted and the fact that it hardly cooled down at night," said Andreas Matzarakis, professor of environmental meteorology at Freiburg University.

Many people have trouble sleeping on hot nights. Yet, getting enough sleep is important so that the body can recover from the heat and stress of the day.

Matzarakis said that the severity of heat stress was not related solely to air temperatures. Humidity, solar radiation and wind also played a role — and what is known as the 'felt' temperature. He said that humidity and still air could place a heavy strain on the body, even in moderate temperatures.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The less privileged members of society were also among the most vulnerable, said Martin Röösli, environmental scientist at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Basel. "They are more likely to live in homes that are not well insulated or are more likely to work outdoors."

A large proportion of those who died because of the heat probably had only a short life expectancy left, due to their age and medical conditions, but Röösli said that there was a consensus that "some of the deceased could have lived for a long time and were simply in a fragile state at the time of the heat wave."

For Alexandra Schneider, a meteorologist and epidemiologist at the Helmholtz center in Munich in southern Germany, the deaths that occurred during the heat waves were very likely not only because of the "harvesting effect," which describes "how a heat wave causes very vulnerable individuals in particular to die a few days or weeks prematurely."

Had this been the case, there would have been a deficit of mortality in the following weeks, which did not happen. Thus, she believes, a significant proportion of those who died could have lived on for months or even years.

This article was translated from German.

card_2.headline: Trump announces new 'AI force' amid mounting pressure
card_2.article_content:
US President Donald Trump has said he is forming an "AI force," as many, including those from within the industry, have recently sounded the alarm about the dangers of Artificial Intelligence continuing to grow unchecked.

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump said he will announce an "AI czar" to lead the force soon.

The US president continued to brush off warnings about AI's dangers from experts and the AI industry itself as "hoaxes" pushed by the Democrats.

While dismissing warnings about AI, Trump still vowed to be "be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing criminal and civil justice system."

"For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my first term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar,'" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

The US president, who has enjoyed a close relationship with big tech bosses especially during his second term in office, also vowed "not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible Industry," in reference to AI.

"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He described AI as "the next industrial revolution," predicting it will account for 25% of the US GDP.

"We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"

Trump compared the criticism of the unchecked, ultrafast growth of AI to what he called other "hoaxes," listing efforts to impeach him, transgender rights and global warming as examples.

Some of the top names in AI said earlier this week they were working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry.

Industry giants including ChatGPT's OpenAI, Google and Anthropic said they envisioned a self-regulatory body.

The proposal comes amid growing concerns about AI safety, which have escelated in recent weeks, with several AI agents going rogue and breaking into competitors' systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even top names within the industry have raised similar concerns.

Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the industry's development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis all supporting the sentiment.

Trump has dismissed calls to contain AI development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."

Smaller AI companies have meanwhile warned any self-regulatory measures spearheaded by the big names would come at their expense.

card_1.headline: Canada's top general loses election to become head of key NATO Military Committee
card_1.article_content:
Despite a push from the federal government, Canada's chief of the defence staff has lost a vote to be the next chair of the NATO Military Committee, the alliance's top military authority and a key advisory body for its political leaders.

Gen. Jennie Carignan and her German counterpart, Gen. Carsten Breuer, were vying for the position. Top military commanders from NATO's 32 members ultimately decided on Saturday to go with Breuer in a secret ballot election.

The news was announced on social media by the current chair, Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, who congratulated Breuer on his election.

"Your operational judgement, your deep familiarity with this alliance and your leadership of the German Armed Forces will serve NATO well," Dragone said.

A Canadian has not held this position in almost two decades — the last being retired general Ray Henault between 2005 and 2008. Had she won, Carignan would have been the first woman to lead the Military Committee in the 77-year history of the alliance.

In a statement posted to social media, Carignan congratulated Breuer and said, "it was an honour to stand as a candidate and to engage with my fellow Allied Chiefs of Defence throughout this process."

"There is important work ahead for our Alliance, and I know General Breuer will bring strong leadership to his new role. I deeply value the close relationship we have built and look forward to continuing to work together on our NATO initiatives," Carignan added.

EU chief says she wants Canada to become the bloc's 1st associate member

Defence Minister David McGuinty also congratulated Breuer and said on social media that Canada was proud to nominate Carignan, "whose strong candidacy reflected her exceptional leadership, experience and deep commitment to Allied collaboration."

"We remain firmly committed to NATO and our collective defence, and look forward to continuing to work closely with Gen. Breuer and all of our Allies."

Experts who previously spoke to CBC News said a potential roadblock to Carignan winning would be U.S. President Donald Trump — particularly after Prime Minister Mark Carney formally unveiled his intent to strengthen Canada's ties to the European Union.

"Trump is not going to let a Canadian or a woman be the head of the military committee, if anybody around him has paid attention to it," said Steven Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University who's written extensively about NATO.

Canada's top general is up for a senior NATO post. Will Trump get in her way?

Breuer is a 61-year-old army officer who earned the nickname "the chancellor's general" after then-German chancellor Olaf Scholz picked him to lead a crisis committee that helped manage the country's response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021 and 2022.

He joined the Bundeswehr in an air defence unit in 1984, and later attended the U.S. general staff college in Fort Leavenworth, Kan., as well as German general staff training in Hamburg.

German Chief of Defence Gen. Carsten Breuer gives a statement during a Lithuanian-German military exercise in Pabrade, Lithuania, in May 2024. (Mindaugas Kulbis/The Associate Press)

In 2014, Breuer served with NATO's International Security Assistance Force in the Afghan capital Kabul.

Dragone said on social media that Breuer will take office in July 2027.
